Hi,

I made this small Lean project for Daniel Dia’s PROOF101 course. It consists of four definitions (linear code, minimum distance of a code, a code with a lower bound, and Hamming sphere) and two theorems (that the minimum distance of a code equals the minimum of the pairwise distances of its elements, and the disjoint spheres theorem).

You can find the README and the Lean file here:
https://github.com/cduenasnavarro/PROOF101-miniproject-cduenasnavarro

I was wondering whether mathlib would benefit from these definitions and theorems, or some version of them. I think they would belong under Information Theory → Coding, and they rely on Information Theory → Hamming.

If so, I will go through the “How to contribute to mathlib” guidelines. In the meantime, if anyone has insights on whether my definitions or formulations of the theorems would be convenient, or any other feedback, please let me know. Of course, I’ll be happy to credit any help.
Nice job! Let me ask @Wrenna Robson
Interesting. I'm not certain if this is the right definition of not but prepare a PR for sure
I'm not sure if mathlib is the best home for material on coding theory (or perhaps cslib is better, etc.) - but preparing a PR allows discussing your actual code, so go ahead with that for sure!
I don't think it fits into CSLib. Coding theory I would say is squarely mathematics.
Like I learnt it in my maths degree etc.
You know more about this than me - thanks for teaching me!
We will probably need your reviewing help for that one :-)
admittedly Cambridge maths does mix in applied stuff but I would say in practice yeah it's squarely maths
I'm not even a coding theorist really ;_; but yeah I probably am more knowledgeable about this than many
The study of linear codes in particular more or less amounts to packing properties of vector spaces over finite fields in many ways. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_code
They have practical CS and cryptographic applications but so do number theoretic lattices, elliptic curves, etc.

In contrast I would probably say (to choose another area I know about) that hash-based signature schemes and the trees used in their construction are solely CS really. The boundaries are not always clear but essentially my feeling is that there's definitely large parts of information theory and coding theory which is mathematical in character and emphasis even if it then motivates CS approaches and applications.
I believe the ArkLib people have coding theory in their repo so they might also form good reviewers (even if the needs of this for Mathlib are not quite the same).
One thing I do think is important is picking some good and comprehensive sources and using them as the definitive reference.

There are a LOT of books that are intros here. 6949

E.g. here is the ones recommended in the tripos, and I'm not even sure this is a good recommendation set.

It would be appropriate for Mathlib I think to choose a source that is grounded in the mathematical perspective as opposed to TCS (clearly there is some overlap but some sources tend towards one more than the other).
A First Course In Coding Theory by R Hill seems to get recommended a lot and is pitched at the "late undergrad/early graduate" level which feels likely to be appropriate for Mathlib
Definitely worth seeking other opinions though
There are some more specialised works at the coding theory/algebraic geometry border.
J.H. Lint's Introduction to Coding Theory is a little old but is in the Springer "yellow book" tradition of mathematics graduate texts that I think will feel comfortingly familiar to many

I also studied it as a part of my maths master’s degree :)
I agree that we should choose a main book to follow… I used 'Fundamentals of Error-Correcting Codes' by W. Cary Huffman and Vera Pless, 2003, just because it was the main one my teacher used for the class notes. But, in general, I haven’t used Coding theory books much, so I don’t know which one could be followed
I started working on the PR yesterday. Will continue today after work
"Concise Encyclopedia of Coding Theory" might be a good pick. In particular it isn't trying to be a learning resource so much as a reference.

If you're thinking of contributing a subject to mathlib, there's two questions: (a) is it theoretically in scope for a math library and (b) is there a maintainer who can and will review the pull requests (and ideally more than one)
I think there's absolutely no question about a) - it definitely is.
b) is trickier because I don't think we have maintainers from all disciplines
There are several pure mathematical applications of codes, but the construction and analysis of Mathieu’s and Conway’s sporadic simple groups is one that stands out to me.
I didn't know about that - very cool.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Tmx-v4FiP6I and https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dxRf3vHbuoA are nice videos about this (codes and the relation to the sporadic simple groups) if anyone's interested

But also, IIRC coding theory is very related to CS's complexity theory, since error correction goes hand in hand with random complexity. Although, this is also true of expander graphs, but their home is probably mathlib
Yeah I mean fundamentally all this was invented by Shannon when it was still maths, right? But I think the right choice is for Mathlib to enable CSLib downstream

Ruben Van de Velde said:

If you're thinking of contributing a subject to mathlib, there's two questions: (a) is it theoretically in scope for a math library and (b) is there a maintainer who can and will review the pull requests (and ideally more than one)

For (b), for what it's worth I'd be happy to review material in coding theory, I've done some work in that area myself.

Wrenna Robson said:

But I think the right choice is for Mathlib to enable CSLib downstream

I don't understand what this means, could you elaborate?

As in - there is mathematics that naturally has applications to CS, yet is not CS. Instead of saying "that's CS - leave it to CSLib", we should proactively work to add mathematics upstream that will enable those CS applications.
I see, agreed. And FWIW, my experience is the same of having encountered this area during my math undergrad.

+1 for belonging in math as it is very much a discrete combinatorial construction problem (discrete packing) that happens to have applications in electrical engineering (which explains maybe the outsized interest from mathematicians compared to other seemingly similar combinatorial projects). Also, if information theory is already there, this is the basically the constructive (lower bounds) side of the same problems.

Maybe a oversight on someones part, but I did get a PhD in pure math by working on error-correcting codes from algebraic curves.

I think working up to https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enumerator_polynomial#MacWilliams_identity would be awesome. If I remember correctly there is a neat proof using finite representation theory, that would be well suited for mathlib - favoring short proofs assuming other branches of math, instead of textbook proofs that cannot do so.

Always happy to chat if someone needs help on this, though I am not a Lean expert and at this point not a coding theory expert either.

Some more books on coding theory (sadly, I don't remember which one I liked):

  • https://archive.org/details/introductiontoco0000lint
  • probably too advanced for this project - https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-540-76878-4 but this has the connection with function fields and number theory for constructing codes from algebraic curves, which turns out have the best asymptotic bounds.
@Rado Kirov we don't have much information theory - I created that folder as an aspiration some years ago ;)

Ah, that makes more sense. Anyways, maybe how mathlib handles elliptic curves can be used as example to follow for coding theory, as there is also a continuum from deep theoretical math to pure application.
I think that would make sense

@Cristina Dueñas Navarro are you aware of docs#Set.infsep
I created it for just this day :D
it is "minDist", essentially.
It gives you the minimum distance of any two distinct members of a set.
docs#Set.einfsep is the extended version (which behaves a little betetr)
I strongly recommend using it as I think it will make stating and proving your stuff much easier, though I think there's an argument for defining minDist as a synonym in this particular case.
This genuinely feels like a bit of a "plans are measured in centuries" moment if you do use it because I created it knowing that one day we would need it for coding theory.
The codamain of mindist is N (everything in coding theory is finite and discrete) while infsep is R. Not sure of that would cause issues further down.
Indeed so - this was actually one of the things that made my original efforts foul up a little, capturing this.
But you could coerce it to N quite easily, and thereafter prove that it has the right properties.
(We lack a way of describing an integer-valued metric.)
What does graph theory do? Like how do they define diameters, and other distance on a graph notions. Coding theory can be seen as combinatorial problems on the hamming cube graph.
However - also, many theorems are true for any integer-valued metric - they aren't theorems about codes.
I think they don't do things in the same way because it's more clearly discrete.

I do think a theory of Nat-valued metrics would frankly be helpful in lots of discrete maths settings but, as I say, I made no progress getting interest from maintainers on it when I last explored the issue.

This having been said, Set.Nontrivial.infsep_lt_iff is a good example of a theorem that nearly gets you all the way to where you might need. It is good to be precise about when exactly you need the fact the dist is integral.

Rado Kirov said:

docs#SimpleGraph.edist: G.edist u v := ⨅ w : G.Walk u v, (w.length : ℕ∞)

My feeling is that if we're not going to define a general theory of Nat-valued metrics, the thing to do is just make a particular definition for codes, but use infsep for it

It's worth saying that really all the properties you want for infsep are not really about it being int valued itself so much as the metric is int valued and the underlying space being finite means the infimum is a real minimum
These are two separate properties
Though I suppose it's also true that it being integer valued does actually also mean that of the infimum
I struggled to capture the general property though
"real minimum" sounds like docs#IsWellFounded or (the linear order version) docs#IsWellOrder

if the maths is indifferent to a Nat-valued metric vs a {Even Nat}-valued metric, the combination of conditions (besides ordered additive monoid) might be

  1. N is docs#WellFoundedLT (i.e. no infinite descending chains)
  2. every Iic n : Set N is docs#WellFoundedGT (i.e. no bounded infinite ascending chains)
  3. linear/total order
if you relax #2 then you're dealing with an docs#IsWellOrder, but the addition might be difficult to work with
If you relax #3 then you get constructions like finitely supported "distributions" {f : ι → ℕ // Finite (f^-1 (Ici 1)) } (or finite multisets, if you prefer)
In that case, monotone addition means you're working in a SemilatticeSup

Chris C said:

If you relax #3 then you get constructions like finitely supported "distributions" {f : ι → ℕ // Finite (f^-1 (Ici 1)) } (or finite multisets, if you prefer)

there is docs#Multiset
there's also probably weirder constructions without a well behaved additive basis, like {f : ℕ → ℕ | f nondecreasing, upper bounded [i.e. O(1)]}

Hi! Sorry, I haven’t been able to look at it yet. Thanks for the new insights. I'll get to it soon.
@charisios koutsonas and I were wondering whether it would be better to define in my PR variable (F : Type*) [Field F] [Fintype F] [DecidableEq F] with Type instead of Type*. I don't think we actually need Type*, although it's commonly used.

Type* is strongly preferred over Type because it makes your declarations universe-polymorphic. Using Type here constrains F to live in a particular universe, which can cause issues down the line. Best practice is to use Type* unless you have a good reason not to.
